content: ScienceNet is an experimental search engine developed at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) by the Liebel-Lab. It is specifically designed to facilitate access to scientific knowledge. The software that powers ScienceNet, known as YaCy, is built on peer-to-peer (P2P) technology. This technology was developed by Michael Christen in collaboration with the Liebel-Lab at KIT. Scientific knowledge is currently dispersed across numerous databases, research institutions, educational websites, and literature repositories. Modern search engines often rely on popularity-based ranking systems to deliver results. While this approach is effective for general search purposes, it is less suitable for retrieving scientific information. ScienceNet addresses this limitation by focusing exclusively on indexing scientific websites and content, such as those from the German Helmholtz Society, Max Planck Institutes, and universities in Switzerland and Austria. This focus distinguishes ScienceNet from the global YaCy search engine, known as Freeworld, which serves as a general-purpose search engine. The architecture of ScienceNet consists of a network of Linux-based PCs running the YaCy software. The core cluster of ScienceNet is hosted at the Institute of Toxicology and Genetics (Liebel-Lab) at KIT. The system has been designed and tested to operate efficiently in a network comprising at least 2,000 CPUs. Each CPU is capable of indexing up to 10 million web pages, enabling the search engine to handle large-scale and distributed information repositories. The mission of ScienceNet is to encourage universities and research institutions to adopt the software and contribute to the scientific network. The software automatically connects to the core cluster and integrates its search engine capabilities into the distributed ScienceNet network. To participate, institutions require a high-speed broadband internet connection (greater than 2 Mbit/s) and dedicated PCs. Ideally, each research institute would run the free YaCy-ScienceNet software on one or two local PCs and make its web pages available to the network. This approach not only enhances the network but also minimizes bandwidth waste caused by external search engines. The ultimate goal of ScienceNet is to provide the scientific community with a free and open search engine index. By leveraging a distributed peer-to-peer network, ScienceNet aims to index millions of documents and make them accessible to researchers and institutions worldwide.
